slip/path: With a chain of thought, a model writes its steps before its answer. Asked for seventeen times twenty four, it finds three hundred and forty, then sixty eight, and adds them: four hundred and eight.
slip/slip: But every step is a chance to slip. Get seventeen times four wrong, as fifty eight, and the steps after it carry the slip all the way to a wrong answer: three hundred and ninety eight.
slip/sample: And with sampling, which path you get is luck. At a temperature above zero, each run picks its tokens at random, so each run takes its own route. Sample five of them.
slip/scatter: Three reach four hundred and eight, by three different routes. The two slips land apart: one at three hundred and ninety eight, one at four hundred and eighteen.
slip/agree: That is the pattern. There is one right answer, so right paths pile up on it. A slip can land anywhere, so wrong paths seldom agree with each other.
vote/count: So ignore the routes, and count only the final answers: one vote per run.
vote/win: Four hundred and eight has three votes of five, the most, so it is the answer returned. It is right, even though two of the runs went wrong.
vote/name: This is self-consistency. The answer it returns is the one the model's own samples are consistent about, and that is where the name comes from.
vote/wang: In 2022, Shweh-jer Wahng and colleagues at Google proposed it, in place of the single greedy path that chain of thought had used. Their bet: right reasoning, however varied, agrees on its final answer more often than wrong reasoning does.
vote/gain: On grade-school math word problems, one large model solved fifty six and a half percent with its greedy path. Voting over forty sampled paths, it solved seventy four point four percent.
needs/greedy: The vote needs real sampling. As the temperature goes toward zero, sampling turns greedy: every run takes the most likely token at every step.
needs/copies: So all five runs write the same path and reach the same answer. Five copies of one answer give the vote nothing to choose between.
needs/compare: And it needs final answers that can be compared: a number, a letter, yes or no. Wang's team said as much: the answer has to come from a fixed set.
needs/stories: Five stories about a lighthouse never match word for word. Each gets one vote, and there is no majority to find.
try/p1: Try one. Asked for fifteen percent of eighty, a model samples seven chains of thought. Their final answers are fifteen, twelve, twelve, eight, twelve, fifteen and twelve. What does self-consistency return?
try/a1: Count each answer: twelve four times, fifteen twice, and eight once. Twelve has the most votes, four of seven, so twelve is returned.
try/not: Not the first path's fifteen: that is one path. And not the average, about twelve point two nine: a number no path reached.
try/p2: Now each of five replies to a multiple-choice question ends in a letter, A to D. Can the vote pick a better reply than one sample?
try/a2: Yes. Different paths often end on the same letter, so letters can be counted. Here three of the five end in B, so B wins.
